display_title: Response to Reviewer DBgb. Thank you for your comments!

content.title: Response to Reviewer DBgb. Thank you for your comments!
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback. Below are the responses to each comment. 

**1. Re: With different target prefix, the claimed connection could be weak.**

We respectively disagree that the connection between exposure bias and modality gap is weak because of different target prefixes. For auto-regressive models, there are two factors that influence the behaviour of the model during inference: source-side input $x$ and target-side prefix $y_{<i}$. If we only consider the input differences (speech or text), it is equivalent to considering only the situation at training time (teacher forcing), which is not the same as inference. To understand the difference between ST and MT during inference, we believe it is necessary to consider both input and target prefix in the modality gap. Besides, the target prefixes of ST and MT are not unrelated. They are progressively different over time due to the modality gap, which in turn enlarges the modal gap. That's why we observe that the modality gap keeps increasing during inference. This connection between the modality gap and exposure bias has greatly inspired our approach, which finally proved to be effective in reducing the modality gap and improving the performance of ST.

**2. Re: The novelty is limited as the proposed method is a combination of three existing techniques.**

Our approach is based on three existing techniques, but we would argue that our approach is not a simple combination of them. Actually, those three techniques were proposed to address different problems in NMT. For example, scheduled sampling was proposed to alleviate the exposure bias, regularization was proposed to prevent over-fitting, and token-level adaptive training was proposed to tackle the token imbalance problem. However, in this work, we just focus on the problem of modality gap in ST. Based on our preliminary study, we are motivated to combine those three techniques together, which has proven to be effective in alleviating the modality gap and improving the performance of ST.

In addition, as shown in Table 2, simply applying one of those three techniques does not work well. For example, scheduled sampling usually does not work well for seq2seq model, and we did observe only a 0.1 BLEU improvement. Meanwhile, just regularizing the output of ST and MT only yields an improvement of 0.5 BLEU. However, combining them together can create the "one plus one greater than two" effect of 1.1 BLEU improvement, because it exactly alleviates the modality gap during inference. Besides, the token-level adaptive training can help the model deal with cases with large modality gap, which brings further 0.4 BLEU improvement. In summary, we believe our method is well motivated rather than a simple combination, and achieves state-of-the-art ST performance.

We would appreciate it if you could reevaluate the novelty of our method. As other reviewers said:
- Reviewer AjE3: All three ideas are not really new individually, but their combination and their application to the problem of closing the modality gap in ST is both new and unexpected
- Reviewer aE1Y: Analyzing modality gap from the MT and ST decoder layer, provides an in-depth findings, and is an input for creating a truly multimodal model
- Reviewer 1Vmc: SS, TAT and Consistency loss had been explored before for MT or other sequence recognition task. Apply it to speech translation and modality matching for encoded speech and text in token level is new.

**3. Re: The comparison in experiments is not fair as the datasets and model structures are different from prior works**

First, the datasets used and model structures of our MTL and CRESS model are consistent with previous SOTA models like XSTNet (Ye et al., 2021), STEMM (Fang et al., 2022), and ConST (Ye et al., 2022). In terms of datasets, we only use LibriSpeech for speech pre-training and MuST-C for ST training in the base setting. We also use the same external MT datasets in the expanded setting (see Appendix A). In terms of model structures, all above models follow the "speech pre-trained model + 2*CNN + Transformer" structure with about 155M parameters. Other methods like STPT (Tang et al., 2022) use larger dataset and larger model. We just display the results from their paper for reference. 

We would emphasize that our MTL system is a strong baseline, which can match the performance of previous systems like XSTNet and STEMM. The comparison between CRESS and MTL is **completely fair**, because the only difference between them is the training strategy. Our CRESS achieves significant improvements over this strong baseline and reaches new state-of-the-art results. We believe this is sufficient to demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our approach.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper combines three methods in order to address the modality gap in end-to-end speech-to-text speech translation (ST), so that multi-task learning with text-to-text machine translation (MT) data can be leveraged more effectively. The proposed CRESS method  combines scheduled sampling, KL-divergence-based cross-modal decoder-state regularization, and token-weighting based on detected modality gaps. One a MuST-C En>XX task, the combined methods significantly outperform a strong multi-task learning baseline, and the reported BLEU scores compare favorably with a number of results reported in other papers.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:

The methods are described clearly, and the BLEU scores look quite good.

The initial analysis of the modality gap in Figures 1 and 2 does a good job of setting up the key contributions of the paper. Returning to that same analysis with the various improvements in place in Figures 4 and 5 was a very nice touch.

The ablations and analysis that are needed to convince me that all three methods are required together are in place.

Hyper-parameter tuning is done on the dev set of a single language pair, and described in careful and replicable detail. For the most carefully tuned parameters, a sensitivity analysis is 
provided on that same dev set. 

Weaknesses:

It is very strange that the authors are already near or above almost all comparison systems with just their MTL system. Furthermore, it’s very strange to see an MTL system doing well at all in their base setting, which uses no additional MT data. Does this really mean that the only text data being used for multi-task learning is the transcriptions of the ST data? IE: that no new semantics or vocabulary items are being introduced by MT data with respect to ST data? The fact that this base system benefits so much from CRESS suggests that this technique’s success has a lot more to do with regularization than it does with having information flow more efficiently across a modality gap, since no new information is being introduced by adding transcripts of speech the system already had access to. I think it would be helpful to show an ST-only baseline to help calibrate the benefit (if any) of doing MTL in this base scenario. It’s possible that the authors have just built a very strong, under-regularized ST baseline and are using text to regularize it.

Along these same lines, I think the paper would be stronger if another experimental condition was investigated (Europarl-ST, CoVoST, etc), so we could see the method working in a different scenario from the one it was developed on, and compared to a different set of methods from the literature.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality:

The proposed methods are reasonable and well-motivated, and the experimental design seems fine, though it would be stronger with another ST dataset included. Some of the MTL and CRESS results in the base setting are hard to explain.

Clarity:

The broad ideas of the paper are very easy to follow. Some specifics are a little fuzzy; for example, what system is used to calculate the divergence gap scores G for token-level adaptive training? The details for development experiments are admirable.

Originality:

All three ideas are not really new individually, but their combination and their application to the problem of closing the modality gap in ST is both new and unexpected.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper presents evidence that modality gap and exposure bias are related, and puts forward a combination of three methods to address this. The results are very strong, but some of the details, especially those pertaining to the base regime with new extra MT data (and therefore little to gain from closing a modality gap) seem a little strange. The paper could be substantially stronger if it included another ST test set.

content.title: Response to Reviewer AjE3. Thank you for your comments!
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback. Below are the responses to each comment. 

**1. Re: It is very strange that the authors are already near or above almost all comparison systems with just their MTL system.**

Honestly speaking, we have made some efforts to build the strong baseline MTL. For example, we use HuBERT rather than Wav2vec 2.0 (see details in Appendix D), and use post-LN rather than pre-LN. Finally, our baseline system can match the performance of XSTNet (Ye et al., 2021), which is the baseline system of previous SOTA ConST (Ye et al., 2022). We believe that developing on a strong baseline will make our results more convincing and demonstrate the robustness of our approach. 

**2. Re: Does this really mean that the only text data being used for multi-task learning is the transcriptions of the ST data?**

The answer is yes. The only data we used in the base setting are the <speech, transcription, translation> triples in MuST-C. To further understand the success of CRESS, we follow your suggestions to add the st-only baseline. Limited by the time and computing resources, now we can provide you with results in 4 translation directions:

| Models      | En-De | En-Fr | En-Es | En-Ro |
| ----------- | ----- | ----- | ----- | ----- |
| ST-only     | 25.2  | 35.5  | 30.5  | 23.9  |
| ST+MT (MTL) | 25.3  | 35.7  | 30.5  | 23.8  |
| CRESS       | 27.2  | 37.8  | 31.9  | 25.9  |

We find that our ST-only baseline is also very strong, which performs comparably with the MTL system. It suggests that simply adding MT task over a strong ST-only baseline does not benefit ST, since no new information is being introduced and the model is not under-regularized. However, the model still cannot handle speech as well as text due to the complexity of speech and the limitations of the model capacity. That's why we observe the representation difference in the top decoder layer between ST and MT. The basic idea of our approach is to reduce this difference with cross-modal regularization. In this way, the knowledge of MT may help ST. However, the simple regularization under teacher forcing does not bring much improvement during inference (+0.5 BLEU). Through our preliminary study, we found the link between the modality gap and exposure bias, and the long-tail problem in the modality gap. Therefore, we introduce scheduled sampling and token-level adaptive training into training. Combining them together, the MT knowledge can flow more efficiently across the modality gap to improve the performance of ST (+1.5 BLEU).

**3. Re: I think the paper would be stronger if another experimental condition was investigated.**

Thanks your suggestions. We conduct experiments on CoVoST 2 dataset with the same configuration as MuST-C. We find that our method can achieve consistent improvements on CoVoST 2 En->De (+1.8 BLEU in the base setting and +1.6 BLEU in the expanded setting). Please check the details in Appendix F in the revised paper.

**4. Re: What system is used to calculate the divergence gap scores G for token-level adaptive training?**

The modality gap $G$ is computed by the model itself on-the-fly. During training, the following steps are performed in sequence: 1. Forward pass of ST and MT, 2. Calculate the modality gap $G$ and the weight $w_i$ for each target token, 3. Calculate the loss in Equation (16)(17)(18), 4. Backward pass.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper propose a speech-translation (ST) approach that leverages both speech and text (MT) input signals. To bridge modality differences (particularly at inference time), authors propose a scheduled sampling regularization technique, that partially leverages the predicted output of  ST and MT tasks along with the ground truth. Moreover, depending on the modality gap between the speech and text, variable weight is assigned on the decoder side at time of training. Experimental results show, the proposed approach outperforming baseline and related works on the MuSTC benchmark.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Compared with MT (text-text translation),  ST (speech-text or speech-speech) tasks suffer from lack of training data. To address data sparsity issue, this work, builds a multi-task model (ST and MT), to primarily leverage the large data set from the MT task. 

Strengthes: 
- preliminary analysis, exploring modality gap b/n ST and MT representations and the analysis (using teacher forcing, beam/greedy search) along with exposure bias  is a strong motivation for the proposed approach. 
- different from previous work, this work follows a fine-grained approach to address the modality gap, that is found to be more visible at time of inference.
- analyzing modality gap from the MT and ST decoder layer, provides an in-depth findings, and is an input for creating a truly multimodal model


Weaknesses
- although, the proposed approach shows the best results in comparison with related work, the fact that the ST data set used is a low-resource setting. It would provide more factual data points if this work includes experimental findings with relatively large ST datasets (e.g. CoVoST2).
- this can be out of scope, however, i don't understand the reason not to report the MT (text-text) translation performance, when claiming the proposed approach is a multi-task/modal model. the same issue is observed in most of the related works.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Quality
- the work is well organized, motivating the problem, discussing the proposed approach, analyzing the experimental results. the writing will benefit from additional proof reading. 

Originality
- although there are ST works that aim to bridge the modality gap between speech and text (recent examples: STEMM (Fang et al., 2022), ConST (Ye et al., 2022)), this work, presents an alternative approach motivated by the preliminary analysis of exposure bias. 

Clarity
- there are multiple statements that require proof reading and fine-tuning the writing of the paper, it would be great if authors focus on using precise words and factual informations (for instance, the sentence "During inference, both ST and MT predict the next token conditioned
on their previous generated tokens, which may be different since the modality gap, thus causing
different predictions.", is hard to understand).
content.summary_of_the_review: Given the preliminary study, that motivated the proposed approach (of leveraging cross-modal regularization and token level adaptive training), this work, presents a novel contribution to the ST literature. Claims are supported by experimental findings, however, experimental results with additional benchmarks can provide more strength for this work.

We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback. Below are the responses to each comment. 

**1. Re: It would provide more factual data points if this work includes experimental findings with relatively large ST datasets.**

Thanks for your suggestions. We conduct experiments on CoVoST 2 dataset. We find that our method can achieve consistent improvements on CoVoST 2 En->De (+1.8 BLEU in the base setting and +1.6 BLEU in the expanded setting). Please check the details in Appendix F in the revised paper.

**2. Re: Not report the MT (text-text) translation performance.**

Thanks for your advice. We have added the results of the MT task to the revised paper (Appendix G). Although improving the MT performance is not our main goal, we surprisingly find that our method can also bring slight improvements for the MT task (+0.3 BLEU). We suggest that this may be due to the regularization effects. We also find that the performance gap between ST and MT is significantly reduced (MTL: 35.0-29.0=6.0, Cress: 35.3-30.3=5.0), which confirms that the improvement in ST is mainly due to the reduction of the modality gap.

**3. Re: It would be great if authors focus on using precise words and factual information.**
Thanks for your suggestions. We have revised some statements in the paper and will further refine the writing.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1Vmc. Thank you for your comments!
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for the helpful feedback. Below are the responses to each comment. 

**1. Re: Does other baseline, the speech encoder also pretrained?**

Sorry for the confusion. Actually, our model architecture is similar to previous state-of-the-art methods, like XSTNet (Ye et al., 2021), STEMM (Fang et al., 2022), ConST (Ye et al., 2022), which combine a pre-trained speech encoder (e.g. Wav2vec 2.0) and a pre-trained MT model. The main difference between our work and previous ones is the training (fine-tuning) techniques of the coupled pre-trained models. For better clarity, we have added markers in Table 1 in the revised paper. 

**2. Re: Literature survey missing some recent work on matching speech text modality.**

Thanks for the reminder. We have added the following papers in the related works:
- [1] SLAM: A unified encoder for speech and language modeling via speech-text joint pre-training.
- [2] mSLAM: Massively multilingual joint pre-training for speech and text.
- [3] MAESTRO: Matched Speech Text Representations through Modality Matching.

**3. Re: The use of "oracle words" is confusing.**

Thanks for your suggestion. To prevent misunderstandings, we use "predicted words" instead of "oracle words" in our revised paper.

**4. Re: Concern about the novelty and advantage of the proposed method.**

**Novelty:** Our approach is based on three existing techniques, but we would argue that our approach is not a simple combination of them. Actually, those three techniques were proposed to address different problems in NMT. For example, scheduled sampling was proposed to alleviate the exposure bias, regularization was proposed to prevent over-fitting, and token-level adaptive training was proposed to tackle the token imbalance problem. However, in this work, we just focus on the problem of modality gap in ST. Based on our preliminary study, we are motivated to combine those three techniques together, which has proven to be effective in alleviating the modality gap and improving the performance of ST.
In addition, as shown in Table 2, simply applying one of those three techniques does not work well. As you said, scheduled sampling usually does not work well for seq2seq model, and we did observe only a 0.1 BLEU improvement. Meanwhile, just regularizing the output of ST and MT only yields an improvement of 0.5 BLEU. However, combining them together can create the "one plus one greater than two" effect of 1.1 BLEU improvement, because it exactly alleviates the modality gap during inference. 

**Advantages:** The main advantages of our approach are low training costs and high performance. For example, XSTNet (Ye et al., 2021) and ConST (Ye et al., 2022) are based on progressive training, which introduces large-scale MT dataset during fine-tuning, making the training time much longer. STEMM (Fang et al., 2022) performs word-level mixup between speech and text, which requires external alignment tools (e.g., Montreal Forced Aligner) to obtain the alignment between speech and text before training, introducing additional overhead and possible error propagation. STPT (Tang et al., 2022) jointly pretrain on speech and text with large-scale data (60k hours speech, ASR, MT), and thus has a large training cost. In contrast, our method does not require any additional pre-processing, and the training speed is almost the same as the MTL baseline (See details in Appendix C). At the same time, our method beats all of the above methods in all 8 directions on MuST-C dataset. 

**5. Re: Concern about the significance of the results.**

We did experiments on all 8 directions of MuST-C dataset, in both the base and expanded settings. We evaluate our system with both sacreBLEU and ChrF++ scores with significant tests (Table 1 and 5), demonstrating the significance of the results. Following your suggestions, we conduct experiments on CoVoST 2 dataset. We find that our method can achieve consistent improvements on CoVoST 2 En->De (+1.8 BLEU in the base setting and +1.6 BLEU in the expanded setting). Please check the details in Appendix F in the revised paper.

content.title: Thank you for your feedback and increasing the score!
content.comment: We believe that our claims are well supported by the experimental results. For "one plus one greater than two effect", we observe that only scheduled sampling or regularization show limited improvements (+0.1 and +0.5 BLEU, respectively), but combining them together gives a more significant improvement (+1.1 BLEU). On the one hand, scheduled sampling is used for alleviating the exposure bias, but the modality gap cannot be reduced without the regularization loss. On the other hand, regularization with teacher forcing can bridge the modality gap between ST and MT during training. However, it cannot help much during inference, as it does not alleviate the cascading effects due to the modality gap. If we combine both together, scheduled sampling can approximate the inference mode, and regularization can bridge the modality gap. This allows for more consistent predictions between ST and MT during inference, so the improvement for ST is much more significant. That's why we believe that our method can create the "one plus one greater than two" effect. For "exactly alleviates the modality gap during inference", we have explained this intuitively in the above. Experimentally, we observed the curves of the modality gap with decoding steps (Figure 5 in the paper), and found that our approach significantly slows down the increase of the modality gap compared with the baseline, which can also support our claim.
